source: Drive 'Computing Overview' Year 9 (Python Programming Revisited) and the Y9 lesson plan example 'Programming basics: data types and operations' (AQA 8525 Unit 2A style), adapted to Python and to the Edexcel 1CP2 Topic 6 style (pseudo-code and Python) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9, v3): Tarbiyyah Secondary Computing and ICT Curriculum Intent, Year 9 (computer systems and architecture), previewing Pearson Edexcel 4CP0 Topic 3; weekly Python retrieval starter

lessons.title: Input, output, variables and data types
objectives: Use print and input to communicate with a user in Python
Declare and assign variables with sensible names
Name and use the data types integer, real (float), Boolean, character and string

keywords.def: a named location in memory that stores a value
the kind of data stored, such as integer or string
a whole number, for example 7
a sequence of characters, for example 'Salam'
changing data from one type to another

starter: Bismillah. What is a variable in Scratch? Give an example from last year.
Is the number 3.5 a whole number?
What is the difference between an input and an output?

teach.heading: Print and input
bullets: name = input('Your name? ') stores a reply.
teach.note: Open IDLE or an online Python editor. Type the two lines and run them. Colour coding in IDLE helps pupils spot strings. Misconception: input() gives a number if the user types digits; it always returns a string, so casting is needed.

teach.heading: Data types
teach.note: Show type(x) in the shell for each. Note: Python has no separate character type; a character is a string of length 1, but in exam questions a character is one symbol. A string can contain digits but is not a number: '5' is not 5.

teach.heading: Casting
teach.note: Live-code: age = input('Age? ') then age + 1 causes an error. Fix with int(age) + 1. Ask pupils to read the error message. Debugging is a skill: read the message from the bottom up.

teach.heading: Pseudo-code and Python
teach.note: Show pseudo-code beside Python for the same program. At GCSE, algorithms in written papers appear as flowcharts and pseudo-code while programming is in Python, so we practise translating. Keep names meaningful: total_price rather than x.

practice: What data type is each: 17, 'Maryam', 3.5, True, '17'?
What is the output? name = 'Yusuf' then print('Salam ' + name). (Salam Yusuf)
Fix the bug: age = input('Age? ') then print(age + 1). (use int(age) + 1)
independent: Write a program that asks for the user's name and favourite number and prints a sentence using both.
Write a program that asks for two decimal numbers and prints their average.
Stretch: write a program that asks for a price and a quantity and prints the total cost, formatted with 2 decimal places.
exit: What data type does input() return?
Write the Python to convert the string '8' to an integer.
lessons.homework: Write a program that asks for a user's name and age and prints how old they will be in 10 years. Write down the data type of each variable.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a data type matching card and Python code to fill in; pair programming. Stretch: explain what happens when float('abc') runs and how a program might avoid crashing.

lessons.title: Arithmetic: DIV, MOD and operations
objectives: Use +, -, *, / and the integer division and modulus operators
Explain the difference between / and // (DIV) and % (MOD)
Solve problems using DIV and MOD

keywords.def: division that gives only the whole-number part, written // in Python
the remainder after division, written % in Python
a symbol that carries out an operation
raising to a power, written ** in Python

starter: Bismillah. What is the output of: x = 4, y = 3, print(x * y)?

teach.heading: Operators in Python
teach.note: Run 7 / 2 (3.5) and 8 / 2 (4.0) in the shell. Misconception: pupils expect 8 / 2 to be an integer; in Python 3 it is a float 4.0.

teach.heading: DIV and MOD
teach.note: Use a 'how many full weeks in 31 days' context. 31 days is 4 full weeks and 3 days left. Mod gives remainder, not a percentage: a common misconception, especially because the symbol % looks like percent. Ensure pupils know DIV and MOD as exam words even though Python writes // and %.

teach.heading: Real uses of MOD
bullets: Convert minutes: 135 minutes is 2 h 15 min.
teach.note: Work the minutes example on screen: hours = 135 // 60, minutes = 135 % 60. Use prayer-time style questions: Fajr is at 05:30 and Dhuhr at 13:05, so how many minutes between? 455 minutes, 7 h 35 min. Pupils practise converting.

teach.heading: Order of operations
teach.note: Use the example 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 and (2 + 3) * 4 = 20. Show that expressions are evaluated by precedence in Python as in maths. Ask pupils to predict before running.

practice: A box holds 12 eggs. How many full boxes from 100 eggs, and how many left over? (8 boxes, 4 left)
independent: Write a program that asks for a number of seconds and prints it as minutes and seconds using // and %.
Write a program that asks for a whole number and prints 'even' or 'odd' using %.
Stretch: write a program which asks for pence and prints how many pounds and pence that is.
lessons.homework: Write a Python program that converts a number of days into weeks and days. Test with 100 days (14 weeks, 2 days).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a worked example sheet with DIV and MOD shown as groups of counters. Stretch: use % to check whether a year is divisible by 4 and explain why this is not enough for leap years.

lessons.title: Selection: if, elif, else and Boolean logic
objectives: Use comparison operators to write Boolean expressions
Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT
Write programs using if, elif and else

keywords.def: a program structure that chooses between paths based on a condition
a condition that evaluates to True or False
one structure placed inside another
spaces at the start of a line which show which block of code it belongs to

starter: Is 'age >= 13' True when age is 13? Why?
Name the three programming constructs: sequence, ___, iteration.

teach.heading: Comparison operators
teach.note: Emphasise that = assigns and == compares. This is one of the most common syntax errors. Run quick shell checks: 5 == 5, 5 != 5, 7 >= 7.

teach.heading: if, elif, else
bullets: elif checks another if the first is False.
teach.note: Live-code a grade program: score >= 70 'Distinction', score >= 50 'Merit', else 'Pass'. Explain that Python checks from the top and stops at the first True condition. Indentation is part of the syntax: four spaces.

teach.heading: AND, OR, NOT
teach.note: Use a truth table. Example: if age >= 11 and age <= 16: print('Secondary pupil'). Python also allows 11 <= age <= 16, but stay with the 'and' form because it works in other languages and in exam pseudo-code. Link to logic gates which appear later in the course.

teach.heading: Pseudo-code version
teach.note: Show pseudo-code and Python side by side. Ask pupils to trace it for scores 49, 50 and 51. Boundary values (49, 50, 51) are the key test cases. Introduce the idea of test data: normal, boundary and erroneous.

practice: Evaluate: (4 > 2) and (3 == 3), (4 < 2) or (3 == 3), not (4 > 2). (True, True, False)
Trace the grade program for 70, 69 and 50. (Distinction, Merit, Merit)
Correct the error: if score = 50: print('Pass'). (use ==)
independent: Write a program which asks for a score out of 100 and prints a grade using if, elif and else.
Write a program that asks for a day number (1 to 7) and prints whether it is Jumu'ah (day 5, with Monday as 1), the weekend or a weekday.
Stretch: write a ticket price program using age and whether the person is a student, with nested if statements.
exit: What is the difference between = and ==?
Give three test values for a program that checks score >= 50.
lessons.homework: Write a program that asks for a password and prints 'Access granted' if it matches a stored password, else 'Access denied'. List three test cases.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a flow diagram and colour-coded code blocks to reorder. Stretch: add input validation that rejects scores below 0 or above 100.

lessons.title: Iteration: while loops and for loops
objectives: Use while loops for condition-controlled iteration
Use for loops with range for count-controlled iteration
Trace a loop and use it to validate input

keywords.def: repeating a set of instructions
repeats while a condition is True
repeats a set number of times
a loop which never stops because its condition never becomes False

starter: Bismillah. Write an if statement that prints 'Adult' when age >= 18.
What is the difference between selection and iteration?
Why might we need to repeat part of a program?

teach.heading: For loops
bullets: for i in range(5): runs 5 times.
teach.note: Run for i in range(1, 6): print(i). Ask pupils what range(1, 6) gives: 1 to 5, not 6. Misconception: the end value is included; it is not. Count-controlled iteration is used when the number of repeats is known.

teach.heading: While loops
bullets: Change something inside so it can end.
teach.note: Live-code a password loop or a countdown: count = 3, while count > 0: print(count), count = count - 1. Show the effect of forgetting count = count - 1 (infinite loop, stop with Ctrl+C). Link to Year 5 'repeat until'.

teach.heading: Validating input
bullets: Ask for a number from 1 to 10.
While the number is outside the range:
teach.note: Write: n = int(input('1-10? ')), while n < 1 or n > 10: n = int(input('Try again: ')). Introduce validation as checking that input is sensible. Say input validation is not the same as verification (checking it is correct). Use the example of an age field.

teach.heading: Tracing a loop
bullets: for i in range(1, 4): total = total + i.
teach.note: Draw the trace table on screen with columns i and total. Pupils fill it with you. Teach that careful tracing is the key skill for finding bugs and is tested in written exams.

practice: What does for i in range(2, 6): print(i) print? (2, 3, 4, 5)
How many times does 'while x < 3' run if x starts at 0 and increases by 1 each time? (3)
Spot the bug: count = 5, while count > 0: print(count). (count is never reduced: infinite loop)
independent: Write a program that prints the 7 times table from 1 x 7 to 12 x 7 using a for loop.
Write a program which keeps asking for a password until the user types the correct one (use a while loop).
Stretch: write a program that asks for 5 numbers and prints the total and the average.
exit: Which loop would you use when you do not know how many repeats are needed?
Complete the trace: total = 0; for i in range(1, 5): total = total + i. What is total at the end? (10)
lessons.homework: Write a program using a loop to print the first 10 square numbers (1, 4, 9 ... 100). Include a comment explaining each line.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide code skeletons with blanks and a trace table template. Stretch: write a nested loop that prints a 5 by 5 multiplication grid.

lessons.title: Hardware and software; input, output and storage
lessons.bigQuestion: A smartphone, a washing machine and a car all contain computers. What do they have in common?
objectives: To understand how hardware and software work together in a computer system
successCriteria: All: sort examples into hardware and software
Most: classify devices as input, output or storage
Some: explain the difference between system software and application software
lessons.smsc: Moral: e-waste and the amanah of the earth's resources when devices are thrown away

keywords.def: the physical parts of a computer you can touch
programs and data that run on the hardware
hardware that sends data into a computer
hardware that presents results from a computer
keeping data so it can be used again later

hook.text: A smartphone, a washing machine and a car all contain computers. What do they have in common?
hook.a: Each has hardware, runs software, takes input, processes it and gives output.

starter.a: A precise sequence of steps to solve a problem.

teach.heading: Hardware and software
teach.note: A laptop with no software is a box of parts; software needs hardware to run on.

teach.heading: Input, process, output, storage
teach.note: Model of a computer system.

teach.heading: Sort the devices
bullets: A touchscreen is input and output
teach.note: Card sort.

teach.heading: Two kinds of software
bullets: System software runs the computer: operating system, utilities
Application software does a user's task: word processor, browser
teach.note: Teams is application software; Windows is system software.

right.title: Application software
points: Does a task for the user

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: A browser does a task for the user; the others manage the computer (system software).

practice.q: Is a touchscreen input, output or both? Explain.
practice.a: Both: it detects touches (input) and displays images (output).
practice.model: Teacher asks two questions of the device: does data go in? yes, touches. Does data come out? yes, the display. So both.

practice.q: Classify: spreadsheet program, antivirus, operating system.
Name the part of the system that processes data.

independent.q: Core: For a smart doorbell, list its inputs, process, outputs and storage in the portal response box.
independent.a: Inputs: button, camera, microphone; process: chip decides to notify; outputs: chime, phone alert; storage: saved clips.
independent.model: Teacher completes the inputs row aloud.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why a computer needs both hardware and software, using an example.
independent.a: Hardware provides the physical means to compute; software gives the instructions. A laptop with no OS cannot run Teams.

independent.q: Stretch: A device driver is system software. Explain what it does.
independent.a: It lets the operating system communicate with a specific piece of hardware, such as a printer.

exit.q: A webcam is... A) an output device B) an input device C) storage
Big question: what do a smartphone, washing machine and car computer have in common?
exit.a: Hardware running software, with input, processing, output and storage.

lessons.homework: List five devices at home that contain a computer and name one input and one output for each.
lessons.send: SEND: device picture cards for the sort. EAL: hardware, software, input, output glossary. Stretch: research embedded systems.

lessons.title: The CPU and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
lessons.bigQuestion: A 3 GHz processor does 3 billion cycles every second. What is it actually doing in each one?
objectives: To understand how the CPU carries out instructions using the fetch-decode-execute cycle
successCriteria: All: name the parts of the CPU (control unit, ALU, registers)
Most: describe the three stages of the cycle in order
Some: explain how clock speed and the number of cores affect performance
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: standard form for billions (3 x 10^9)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the precision in creation compared with the best human-made machines (al-Mulk 67:3-4)

keywords.def: central processing unit: carries out instructions
arithmetic logic unit: does calculations and logic
directs the flow of data and decodes instructions
a tiny, very fast store inside the CPU
how many cycles the CPU does per second, in GHz

hook.text: A 3 GHz processor does 3 billion cycles every second. What is it actually doing in each one?
hook.a: Fetching, decoding and executing instructions, one small step at a time.

starter.q: Python: what is the data type of 3.5?
Is a printer input or output?
Name one piece of system software.

teach.heading: Inside the CPU
teach.note: Registers to name: program counter (PC, address of next instruction), memory address register (MAR), memory data register (MDR), accumulator.

teach.heading: Fetch
bullets: Instruction fetched from RAM to MDR
teach.note: Emphasise the PC increasing so the next instruction is ready.

teach.heading: Decode and execute
bullets: Execute: ALU calculates, or data is moved
teach.note: Repeats billions of times a second.

teach.heading: Performance
bullets: Clock speed: more cycles per second
Cache: fast memory close to the CPU
teach.note: More cores help only if software can split the work.

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Up to twice as many cycles per second
More tasks at the same time

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction?
check.why: The PC points to the next instruction; the MDR holds the data fetched; the ALU is not a register.

practice.q: Describe the fetch stage in two sentences.
practice.a: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR and the instruction at that address is fetched from RAM into the MDR. The PC is increased by 1.
practice.model: Teacher writes it in two sentences, naming each register as it is used.

practice.q: Which part of the CPU adds two numbers?
What does 3.2 GHz mean?

independent.q: Core: Put the 6 cards of the cycle in order and write one sentence for each stage (worksheet).
independent.a: PC to MAR; fetch to MDR; PC + 1; decode in CU; execute; repeat.
independent.model: Teacher places card 1 (PC address copied to MAR) and explains it.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why doubling the cores does not always double the speed.
independent.a: Some tasks cannot be split into parts that run at the same time, and cores share memory.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why cache makes a CPU faster.
independent.a: Cache stores frequently used data close to the CPU, so it waits less for slower RAM.

exit.q: The stages in order are... A) decode, fetch, execute B) fetch, decode, execute C) execute, fetch, decode
Big question: what is the CPU doing in each cycle?
exit.a: Fetching an instruction from memory, decoding it and executing it.

lessons.homework: Look up your home computer or phone's processor: clock speed and number of cores. Write what each tells you.
lessons.send: SEND: cycle cards with pictures. EAL: fetch, decode, execute glossary. Stretch: research von Neumann architecture.

lessons.title: Memory and storage: RAM, ROM and secondary storage
lessons.bigQuestion: When the power cuts out, your unsaved essay is lost but your saved files are not. Why?
objectives: To understand the different roles of RAM, ROM and secondary storage
successCriteria: All: state that RAM is volatile and ROM is non-volatile
Most: compare magnetic, solid state and optical storage
Some: choose suitable storage for a scenario and justify it
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: magnetism (hard disks) and light (optical discs)
lessons.smsc: Moral: backing up and keeping others' data safe as a trust

keywords.def: random access memory: holds programs and data in use; volatile
read-only memory: holds the start-up instructions; non-volatile
loses its contents when the power is off
keeps data permanently, such as an SSD or hard disk
how much data a device can store

hook.text: When the power cuts out, your unsaved essay is lost but your saved files are not. Why?
hook.a: Unsaved work is in RAM, which is volatile; saved files are on secondary storage, which is not.

starter.q: What are the three stages of the CPU cycle?
Which register holds the address of the next instruction?

teach.heading: Main memory
bullets: RAM: programs and data in use
teach.note: More RAM lets more programs run at once.

teach.heading: Why secondary storage?
bullets: We need to keep files and programs
teach.note: Save to OneDrive (school Microsoft 365) as well as the device.

teach.heading: Types of secondary storage
bullets: Solid state: SSD, USB stick, SD card
teach.note: Compare.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which memory loses its contents when the power is off?
check.why: RAM is volatile; ROM, SSD and DVD keep their data.

practice.q: Why is the boot program stored in ROM, not RAM?
practice.a: ROM is non-volatile, so the start-up instructions are there when the power comes on.
practice.model: Teacher reasons: when the computer starts, RAM is empty because it is volatile; the CPU needs instructions at once, so they must be in non-volatile ROM.

practice.q: Which storage for a phone: HDD or SSD? Why?
practice.a: SSD: small, fast, no moving parts so it survives drops.

practice.q: Give one advantage of cloud storage.
practice.a: Access from any device; backed up off-site.

independent.q: Core: Choose storage for: a photographer's 4 TB archive; a pupil carrying homework; a school laptop. Justify each in the portal response box.
independent.a: HDD (cheap per GB, large); USB flash drive or OneDrive (portable); SSD (fast, robust).
independent.model: Teacher justifies the photographer: large capacity needed, cost matters more than speed, so HDD.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why adding RAM can make a computer faster.
independent.a: More programs and data fit in RAM, so less is swapped to slower secondary storage (virtual memory).

independent.q: Stretch: Compare SSD and HDD on speed, durability, capacity and cost.
independent.a: SSD faster and more durable; HDD larger and cheaper per gigabyte.

exit.q: ROM is... A) volatile B) non-volatile
Big question: why is unsaved work lost in a power cut?
exit.a: It is held in RAM, which is volatile.

lessons.homework: Check the storage on a family device: its type (if shown), capacity and how much is free. Back up one important file to OneDrive.
lessons.send: SEND: RAM/ROM comparison table half-filled. EAL: volatile, capacity glossary. Stretch: research virtual memory.

lessons.title: Binary, data units and logic gates
lessons.bigQuestion: A film is 4 GB and a text message about 100 bytes. Roughly how many messages fit in the space of one film?
objectives: To understand how data is measured in units and processed by logic gates
successCriteria: All: order data units from bit to terabyte
Most: convert between units and between binary and denary
Some: complete a truth table for a two-gate circuit
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: powers of 10 and 2, standard form
lessons.smsc: Social: digital storage lets knowledge (including the Qur'an and hadith collections) be shared worldwide

keywords.def: a single 0 or 1
8 bits
1000 bytes (KB); 1024 bytes in the binary convention (KiB)
a component that applies AND, OR or NOT to binary inputs

hook.text: A film is 4 GB and a text message about 100 bytes. Roughly how many messages fit in the space of one film?
hook.a: 4 GB is 4 000 000 000 bytes, so about 40 million messages.

starter.q: Name one type of secondary storage.

teach.heading: Data units
teach.note: Binary prefixes use 1024: 1 KiB = 1024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1024 KiB. Pearson's computer science specifications use the binary prefixes; teach both and use 1024 for exam questions (TO CONFIRM against the 4CP0 specification).

teach.heading: Converting units
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: How many 5 MB photos fit on a 2 GB card?

teach.heading: Gates together
teach.note: Q = (A OR B) AND NOT C.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: How many bits are in 3 bytes?

practice.q: How many 4 MB audio lectures fit on a 1 GB drive?
practice.model: Teacher converts 1 GB to 1000 MB first, then divides by 4.

practice.q: Convert 10100000 to denary.
Convert 2 500 KB to MB.

independent.q: Core: Complete the unit conversions and binary questions on the worksheet (8 questions).
independent.a: Answers on the teacher key.
independent.model: Teacher completes question 1: 3 GB to MB = 3000 MB.

independent.q: Extend: Complete the 8-row truth table for Q = (A OR B) AND NOT C.
independent.a: Q = 1 for rows 010, 100, 110; 0 otherwise.

independent.q: Stretch: A 1920 x 1080 image uses 3 bytes per pixel. Estimate its size in MB.

lessons.title: Operating systems and utility software
lessons.bigQuestion: You have Teams, a browser and a document open at once, but only one processor. How does it cope?
objectives: To understand the functions of an operating system and why utility software is needed
successCriteria: All: name three jobs of an operating system
Most: explain what antivirus, backup and compression utilities do
Some: explain how the operating system manages memory and multitasking
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: protecting devices and data from viruses and scams
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility for protecting shared systems (the school network) from harm

keywords.def: system software that manages hardware and runs programs
how a user interacts with the computer, such as a GUI
programs that maintain and protect the computer
running more than one program at a time

hook.text: You have Teams, a browser and a document open at once, but only one processor. How does it cope?
hook.a: The operating system shares the CPU and memory between programs very quickly (multitasking).

starter.q: Is an operating system system or application software?
Why is the boot program in ROM?

teach.heading: Jobs of an operating system
teach.note: Examples: Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, Linux.

teach.heading: Multitasking and memory
bullets: Programs take turns on the CPU
Virtual memory when RAM is full
teach.note: Turns are so quick it feels simultaneous.

teach.heading: Utility software
bullets: Backup: copies files to keep them safe
teach.note: Defragmentation is not needed for SSDs.

head: Utility
What it does
Why
rows: Rearranges file parts on an HDD

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which utility makes a file smaller to email it?
check.why: Compression reduces file size; the others protect or organise files.

practice.q: Name three functions of an operating system.
practice.a: For example: memory management, file management, user interface.
practice.model: Teacher links each function to something pupils did today: logging in (security), opening Teams (memory and CPU), saving (file management).

practice.q: Why might a school run backups every night?
practice.a: So work can be recovered if a device fails or files are deleted.

practice.q: Why is defragmentation not used on SSDs?
practice.a: SSDs have no moving parts, so access is fast anyway, and it wears the drive.

independent.q: Core: Explain how an operating system lets you use Teams, a browser and a document at once, in the portal response box. Start: 'The operating system...'
independent.a: The operating system shares CPU time between the programs in quick turns and gives each its own memory space; if RAM fills, it uses virtual memory.
independent.model: Teacher writes the first sentence: 'The operating system gives each program a turn on the CPU...'

independent.q: Extend: Compare a GUI and a command-line interface: one advantage of each.
independent.a: GUI: easy for beginners; command line: fast and powerful for experts, uses fewer resources.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why antivirus software must be updated regularly.
independent.a: New malware appears all the time; updates add new signatures so it can be recognised.

exit.q: Which is NOT a job of an operating system? A) memory management B) writing essays C) file management
Big question: how does one processor run three programs at once?
exit.a: The OS shares CPU time between them in very quick turns (multitasking).

Some: choose a primary key and explain why it must be unique

one row: all the data about one item
one column: one type of data
a field that uniquely identifies each record

lessons.title: Searching a database: simple queries
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a shopping website find 'blue shoes under £30' among millions of products?
objectives: To understand how queries use criteria to find records in a database
successCriteria: All: filter a table by one criterion
Most: combine two criteria with AND or OR
Some: write a query in SQL-style form

keywords.def: a question that finds records
the conditions records must meet
show only matching records
a language for querying databases

hook.text: How does a shopping website find 'blue shoes under £30' among millions of products?
hook.a: It runs a query with criteria: colour = blue AND type = shoes AND price < 30.

teach.heading: One criterion
teach.note: Invented example data.

code.text:
SELECT Title
FROM Books
WHERE Pages > 150 AND Available = 'Yes'
code.output:
Tales of the Prophets
Python Basics

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Pages > 150 AND Available = Yes returns how many books from the example?

practice.q: Which books match Pages < 100 OR Available = No?
practice.a: Atlas of the World only (96 pages and not available).
practice.model: I do: check each record: B002 matches both; the others match neither.

independent.q: Filter practice in a spreadsheet: use the 12-record example library data (portal file) to answer five queries and write each in SQL style.
independent.a: Five correct results with SQL-style queries.
independent.model: The teacher runs query 1 with a filter.

independent.q: Extend: write a query to find books with 'Python' in the title.
independent.a: WHERE Title LIKE '%Python%'

independent.q: Stretch: sort the results by Pages, highest first.
independent.a: ORDER BY Pages DESC

exit.q: OR returns records where ...
Back to our ponder: How does a shopping website find 'blue shoes under £30' among millions of products?
exit.a: It runs a query with criteria: colour = blue AND type = shoes AND price < 30.

hook.text: Why might a family with a good income still run out of money each month?
hook.a: Without a plan, small spends add up; a budget shows where money goes.

islamicLink.text: Allah says of the believers: 'And [they are] those who, when they spend, do so not excessively or sparingly but are ever, between that, [justly] moderate' (Al-Furqan 25:67). Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead.
